newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Democracy is key to Yugoslav economy - economists.
newsitem.headline: Democracy is key to Yugoslav economy - economists.

text.p: Serbia's political turmoil has led the country into isolation bringing it close to an economic abyss and the country will collapse without radical democratic changes, economists said on Friday.
They also said official forecasts of the economy growing by as much as 13 percent in 1997 were not only unrealistic but absurd and called for radical and sweeping reforms.
Serbia witnessed three months of mass opposition protests after the ruling Socialists refused to acknowledge the opposition's victory at last November local elections.

"In this country politics dominates the economy. Democratic changes are our only hope. But if the crisis continues, 1997 could become even more catastrophic than 1993," Danilo Sukovic, director of the Economic Resarch Centre of the Institute of Social Science, told Reuters.
Speaking of 1993, when record inflation ran at 60 percent a day, Sukovic said another similar year would be disastrous for the nation which has exhausted most of its reserves.

"There is no way out except for a radical political turn-around. Only then, with a completely new ruling set could Yugoslavia begin to build better relations with the world," said Ljubomir Madzar of the Belgrade School of Economics.
Economists blamed the government for supporting a bankrupt economy, only to buy time and keep social tensions at bay.
"To save the bad ones (companies) means you destroy the good ones, but if this continues, no vital part of the entire economy will be left," Madzar said.
Madzar also cautioned Yugoslavia had been eating up its capital for years without attracting any fresh investment.
"There is a general disbelief in this country, its politics and the economy. And the fact that businessmen do not see any chance of profit Yugoslavia explains why there is no capital flowing in.

"Our external debt plus what the state owes to its people (for old hard currency savings frozen in 1991) amounts to around $15 billion, matching the entire GDP, and our external debt increases by around $800 million a year," Madzar said.

Struggling with inefficiency, illiquidity, surplus labour, inadequate quality, lack of markets and huge fiscal burden, the country's industry recorded in January the third consecutive month of declining output.
The 20.8 percent slump in January versus December buried hopes for any economic revival, economists said.
"We have no more right to losses. Policymakers must establish an alternative economic strategy, in case the main scenario fails," another economist said.
Yugoslavia's government based its optimistic 1997 growth targets on assumptions the country would rejoin the International Monetary Fund (IMF) early in 1997.
"This economy is heading for a collapse. There is no money from domestic sources, so any progress depends on our renewed external borrowing," said another economist.
The expert said a few hundred million dollars, wisely allocated, were sufficient to kick-start the economy currently functioning on barely one billion German marks.
But radical reforms and sweeping privatisation are seen as the key to open up the country and attract foreign capital.
"We are late with reforms, inefficient, there is no genuine privatisation, no economic structure compatible with the rest of the world or one that would secure growth," Sukovic said.

However, one must not flirt with such a serious thing as privatisation, economists said. According to their findings, Serbia was once again rejecting voucher privatisation in a law expected to be discussed in parliament by April.
"Voucher privatisation is the only socially acceptable and just model of privatising the economy," an economist said.
To stress its commitment to reforms, Serbia launched its first ever privatisation ministry, but economists cautioned against the state acquiring too much power over the process.
Analysts also cast doubt on the ministry's readiness for the task which normally requires technical assistance from the IMF and other institutions.
